title.en: The Renewed Eagle and Diuran's Drink
title.zh: 重生的巨鷹與狄烏蘭之飲

region.en: Island of the Eagle, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海巨鷹之島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: On the island of the eagle they find the fifteenth man of the monks of St Brennan of Birr, last survivor of an ocean pilgrimage, with the holy Brennan's tablet. A cloud from the south-west proves an enormous bird, very old, plumage dull and decayed, eating berries from a branch as big as an oak; two eagles come at noon and pick the insects from its jaws and eyes and ears till vespers, and when it is cleansed it plunges in the lake and is renewed — 'thy youth is renewed like the eagle's' — and soars thrice round the island. Diuran bathes and drinks of the lake, and never again knew illness: not a tooth fell from his jaw nor a hair from his head.
summary.zh: 巨鷹島上住著聖布倫南修士團第十五人——海上朝聖的唯一倖存者。西南方一朵「雲」竟是羽色黯朽的蒼老巨鷹，正食橡木大枝上的葡萄狀紅果；正午兩鷹飛來，為其啄去目耳口間蟲豸直至晚禱；洗淨後巨鷹躍入湖中重生——「你的青春如鷹般更新」——繞島三匝而去。狄烏蘭入湖沐浴飲水，此後終身無病：齒不落，髮不脫。

sensitivity.note: The eagle renewed from age to youth is the immram's baptism-of-nature set-piece, glossed with Psalm 103 by the redactor; the healing lake parallels the well of healing of the Fenian cycle (cross-ref the Conn Crither record). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One day they saw what seemed to be a cloud coming up from the south-west. As it drew near, however, they saw the waving of pinions, and perceived that it was an enormous bird. It came into the island, and, alighting very wearily on a hill near the lake, it began eating the red berries, like grapes, which grew on a huge tree-branch as big as a full-grown oak, that it had brought with it. And they saw that it was very old, and its plumage dull and decayed. At the hour of noon two eagles came up from the south-west and alit in front of the great bird, and after resting awhile they set to work picking off the insects that infested its jaws and eyes and ears. This they continued till vespers, when all three ate of the berries again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last, on the following day, when the great bird had been completely cleansed, it plunged into the lake, and again the two eagles picked and cleansed it. Till the third day the great bird remained preening and shaking its pinions, and its feathers became glossy and abundant, and then, soaring upwards, it flew thrice round the island, and away to the quarter whence it had come, and its flight was now swift and strong; whence it was manifest to them that this had been its renewal from old age to youth, according as the prophet said, Thy youth is renewed like the eagle's. Then Diuran said: "Let us bathe in that lake and renew ourselves where the bird hath been renewed." But Diuran plunged in and drank of the water. From that time so long as he lived his eyes were strong and keen, and not a tooth fell from his jaw nor a hair from his head, and he never knew illness or infirmity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Island of the Flaming Rampart

region.en: Island of the flaming rampart, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海烈焰護牆之島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: They come in sight of an island not large, encircled by a rampart of flame that circles round and round it continually; in one part of the rampart there is an opening, and when the opening comes opposite to them they see through it the whole island — men and women, beautiful, many, and wearing adorned garments, with vessels of gold in their hands, and the festal music comes to the ears of the wanderers. For a long time they linger there, watching this marvel, 'and they deemed it delightful to behold.'
summary.zh: 一座不大的島嶼出現眼前，四週烈焰之牆不斷迴旋；牆上有一開口，當開口轉至他們面前，他們便望見全島——眾多俊美的男男女女，衣飾華美，手捧金器，節慶樂聲傳到漂泊者耳中。他們久久滯留凝望此異象，「視之為賞心悅目之奇觀」。

sensitivity.note: The flaming rampart (fire-wall with a turning gate) is the immram's vision of the earthly paradise guarded by fire — the voyage's summit image, kin to the burning wall of the later St Brendan tradition; no landing is permitted. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: They now came in sight of an island which was not large, and it had about it a rampart of flame that circled round and round it continually. In one part of the rampart there was an opening, and when this opening came opposite to them they saw through it the whole island, and saw those who dwelt therein, even men and women, beautiful, many, and wearing adorned garments, with vessels of gold in their hands. And the festal music which they made came to the ears of the wanderers. For a long time they lingered there, watching this marvel, "and they deemed it delightful to behold."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Glass Bridge and the Lady Who Knew No Sin

region.en: Fortress of the glass bridge (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: One of the most elaborately wrought incidents of the voyage: an island with a fortress with a brazen door and a bridge of glass leading to it, which throws the crew backward when they seek to cross; a woman lifts a glass slab from the bridge and lowers her pail into the water beneath, and the melody of the smitten portcullis plunges them in slumber till the morrow, thrice over. On the fourth day she comes out over the bridge in a white mantle with a circlet of gold, and welcomes each man of the crew by his own name; her one pail gives every man what he most desires. Asked in marriage for Maeldun, she answers, 'I know not, nor have ever known, what sin is' — and by morning the island is gone.
summary.zh: 航程中最精緻的一幕：島上有銅門堡壘與一座玻璃橋，眾人欲過橋而橋將其拋回；女子自橋上揭起玻璃板，垂桶取水；敲擊銅閘之聲使他們昏睡至翌晨，如是者三。第四日，她身披白斗篷、金環飾髮，踏橋而出，一一喚出全體船員之名；她的一桶之水，人人得其所願。為梅爾敦提親時她答道：「我不知，也從不知何為罪。」翌晨，島嶼無蹤。

sensitivity.note: The glass bridge that rejects the uninvited is the immram's test-of-worthiness (kin to the glass mountain of later Celtic and Grail lore); the lady who 'knows not what sin is' is the voyage's vision of prelapsarian innocence — the doctrinal Christian overlay on the fairy-mistress motif. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: The island they now reached had on it a fortress with a brazen door, and a bridge of glass leading to it. When they sought to cross the bridge it threw them backward. A woman came out of the fortress with a pail in her hand, and lifting from the bridge a slab of glass she let down her pail into the water beneath, and returned to the fortress. They struck on the brazen portcullis before them to gain admittance, but the melody given forth by the smitten metal plunged them in slumber till the morrow morn; thrice over this happened, the woman each time making an ironical speech about Maeldun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fourth day, however, she came out to them over the bridge, wearing a white mantle with a circlet of gold on her hair, two silver sandals on her rosy feet, and a filmy silken smock next her skin. "My welcome to thee, O Maeldun," she said, and she welcomed each man of the crew by his own name... She gave them abundance of food and drink, all out of her one pail, each man finding in it what he most desired. They do woo the maiden for him, and she replies: "I know not, nor have ever known, what sin is." Twice over this is repeated. "To-morrow, you shall have your answer." When the morning breaks, however, they find themselves once more at sea, with no sign of the island or fortress or lady.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Tuan's History of the Five Invasions
title.zh: 圖安講述的五次入侵史

region.en: Ireland, from Partholon to the Milesians (symbolic pin, Tara)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭：自帕特隆至米利安（象徵定位塔拉）

texts.period: Irish Fairy Tales, James Stephens (1920), Tuan mac Cairill cycle

source.work: James Stephens, Irish Fairy Tales (1920), The Story of Tuan Mac Cairill, eBook #28924

summary.en: Tuan mac Cairill, who watched Ireland's history from every shape he lived through, tells Finnian the tale of the invasions: Partholon and his people who perished of plague; Nemed who fought the Fomor and died of plague; the Firbolgs who came from Spain after the sack of towers and ruled till the Tuatha de Danaan beat them; the gods themselves who held the land until the Milesians came — and Tuan, last of all his kin, saw every age of it, remembering all his births, and told it to the new faith that came with Finnian.
summary.zh: 曾以各種形態親歷愛爾蘭歷史的圖安，向菲尼安講述入侵史：帕特隆一族盡歿於瘟疫；內梅德與弗莫爾交戰而終亡於疫；西班牙出逃的弗博爾格建國，直至神族將其擊敗；諸神居有此地，直到米利安人來臨。圖安——親族中僅存者——目睹每一紀元，銘記每次轉生，將歷史傳予隨菲尼安而來的新信仰。

sensitivity.note: Stephens' retelling of the Lebor Gabala frame through Tuan (a variant of the rebirth record): the five-invasion sequence is the standard Irish origin-list; Tuan as witness merges the rebirth-reincarnation motif with historiographic transmission. Variant record of the same tradition family as the Lebor Gabala chapters. Pin symbolic at Tara.

passages.text: And Tuan told Finnian of the coming of Partholon to Ireland, and of the plague that swept his people from the land, so that not one man of them was left; and of the coming of Nemed, and of his battles with the Fomor, and how his people also died of plague; and of the Firbolgs, who came from Spain after the sack of their towers, and divided Ireland into five provinces, and gave kings to it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, The Story of Tuan Mac Cairill; not verbatim.

passages.text: And he told him of the Tuatha de Danaan, who came out of the north of the world with their four cities and their treasures, and beat the Firbolgs in the first battle, and held Ireland under them till the Sons of Mil came from Spain; and how the gods went into the hills, and the Gael had the land, and Tuan, last of all his kin, watched every age of it, remembering all his births, and told it to the new faith that came with Finnian of the Bells.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, The Story of Tuan Mac Cairill; not verbatim.

title.en: Fionn's First Exploits: the Fianna of the Boyhood
title.zh: 芬恩的初試鋒芒：少年菲亞納

region.en: Tara and the woods of Leinster, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭塔拉與倫斯特林地

texts.period: Irish Fairy Tales, James Stephens (1920), Fenian cycle

source.work: James Stephens, Irish Fairy Tales (1920), eBook #28924

summary.en: Reared in secret in the wilds with his women guardians, Fionn learns his father's enemies wait for his name; he wins the salmon of knowledge, is claimed by the Fianna, and at Tara faces the burning Aillen — but it is Stephens' telling that sets the boy's bonds of hospitality: the boy who is fed must give thanks, the boy who is refused must wander, and the rule of the Fianna that no man shall refuse the asking of any is the law Fionn learns before he wears his father's place.
summary.zh: 芬恩自幼隨女眷隱居荒野，深知父親仇敵候其名而動；他贏得知識之鮭，被菲亞納接納，並在塔拉直面縱火的艾倫。而在斯蒂芬斯的敘事中，少年受的待客之誡尤為醒目：受食者當謝，被拒者當流浪——「任何求助者不可被拒」的菲亞納法典，是芬恩在繼承父位之前先學會的道理。

sensitivity.note: Stephens' version of the Coming of Finn overlaps Gregory's (existing celtic-fionn-boyhood-coming); this record keeps Stephens' hospitality-law frame distinct — the geis of never refusing the asking is the Fianna's charter in this recension. Pin at Tara.

passages.text: Fionn was reared in secret in the wilds, with his women guardians about him, for the enemies of his father waited on his name; and he learned the woods and the water, and the way a boy must hold his tongue and his courage. When the salmon of knowledge was given to him by the poet who had waited seven years for it, he took the wisdom of the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well that is below the sea.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, Irish Fairy Tales; not verbatim.

passages.text: And he learned the law of the Fianna before ever he came to their number: that no man shall refuse the asking of any, that no man shall take cattle by oppression, that no man shall fall back before nine fighting men; and the boy who is fed must give thanks, and the boy who is refused must wander, and these are the rules by which Fionn held the headship of the Fianna of Ireland when his time came.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Stephens 1920, Irish Fairy Tales; not verbatim.
